units.t: Hindsight Bias.
Part one. Nixon's surprise trips.
Think back to a big surprise from the last few years.
An election result, a sporting upset, a market crash, a friend's breakup.
Now ask yourself honestly, did you see it coming?
A lot of people will feel a little voice saying, yes, I sort of did.
This lesson is about that little voice, and why it's so often wrong.
In early 1972, the American president Richard Nixon was about to make historic visits to China and the Soviet Union.
Nobody knew quite what would come of them.
Two researchers in Israel, Baruch Fischhoff and Ruth Beyth, saw an opportunity.
Before the trips, they asked students to estimate the chances of various possible outcomes.
Would Nixon meet Chairman Mao?
Would the trip end with a major new agreement?
Each student put a probability on each event.
After the trips were over, the researchers went back to the same students.
They asked them to remember, as accurately as they could, the probabilities they had given before.
Something odd happened.
For events that had actually occurred, students tended to remember giving higher odds than they really had.
For events that hadn't occurred, they tended to remember giving lower odds.
Their memories had quietly been rewritten to make them look more prescient.
Fischhoff and Beyth published the findings in 1975, under a title that sums it up perfectly.
I knew it would happen.
That same year, Fischhoff ran another clever study.
He gave people a short account of a real but little-known conflict from 1814, between British forces and the Gurkhas of Nepal.
Different groups were told different endings, or no ending at all.
Then everyone was asked how likely each possible outcome had been.
Whatever outcome people were told had happened, they rated as the most likely all along.
And they didn't realise the ending had shaped their judgement.
Fischhoff called this creeping determinism.
Once we know how a story ends, it starts to feel as if it could only ever have ended that way.
This is hindsight bias.
It's the tendency, after something happens, to believe it was more predictable than it really was.
In the next part, we'll see why that isn't just a harmless quirk of memory.
Part two. Learning the wrong lessons.
Why does this happen?
The leading explanation is that our minds are built to make sense of things, not to keep a tidy archive of old opinions.
When we learn an outcome, we fold it straight into our understanding of the world.
Then we search for the causes that led to it, and those causes suddenly look obvious.
The warning signs we'd have dismissed at the time now seem to glow.
After a relationship ends, friends say the signs were all there.
After a share market fall, commentators explain exactly why it had to happen, though very few of them said so the week before.
Once you know the ending, it's almost impossible to unknow it, and to remember how foggy things really looked.
Researchers Neal Roese and Kathleen Vohs have described hindsight bias as working on three levels.
First, memory.
We misremember what we thought before, like Nixon's students.
Second, inevitability.
We come to feel the outcome was bound to happen.
And third, foreseeability.
We feel that we, or someone else, should have known.
That third level is where the real damage is done.
Consider a study by Kim Kamin and Jeffrey Rachlinski, published in 1995.
They asked people to play the role of a council deciding whether to pay for a flood protection measure to protect a nearby business.
One group made the decision looking forward, with only the information available beforehand.
About three quarters of them decided the flood risk was low enough that the precaution wasn't needed.
Another group heard the same facts, plus one extra detail.
A flood had happened, and the business had been damaged.
Now more than half judged the council negligent for not taking the precaution.
Even when a third group was specifically warned about hindsight bias and told to ignore the outcome, the result barely moved.
You can see why this matters.
Doctors, pilots, engineers and managers are all judged after the fact by people who know how things turned out.
In one study from 1981, Hal Arkes and his colleagues gave doctors the same case history, but told different groups different final diagnoses.
Each group thought the diagnosis they'd been given was the one they'd have been most likely to reach themselves.
Hindsight bias also warps how we judge our own decisions.
The former professional poker player Annie Duke calls this resulting.
It's judging the quality of a decision purely by its outcome.
In her book Thinking in Bets, she uses an example from the 2015 Super Bowl, the grand final of American football.
With seconds left and his team one yard from scoring, the Seattle coach Pete Carroll called a passing play.
It was intercepted, and they lost.
The next day, many commentators called it one of the worst decisions in the history of the game.
Duke argues the call was reasonable given the odds, and that if the pass had been caught, the same people might have praised it as a masterstroke.
That's the core problem.
If good outcomes make us think every decision was smart, and bad outcomes make us think every decision was foolish, we learn the wrong lessons.
We might double down on a lucky gamble, or abandon a sound approach that just had one bad break.
So how do you protect yourself from something that rewrites your own memory?
Part three. Keeping yourself honest.
The most powerful fix is also the simplest.
Record your predictions before you know the outcome.
If you're driving right now, don't do anything yet, just file this away for later.
When you make a significant decision, such as taking a new job, making an investment or choosing a school, take a minute once you're parked to jot down or record a quick voice note.
Say what you expect to happen, roughly how confident you are, and why.
Months later, you can compare that note with what really happened, and your memory can't quietly edit it.
The second habit is to ask how things could have turned out differently.
Back in 1977, Paul Slovic and Baruch Fischhoff found that when people were asked to think about how an alternative outcome might have happened, their hindsight bias shrank.
So when you hear yourself saying it was obvious, try building the other story.
What would have had to happen for the result to go the other way?
If you can easily imagine it, the outcome probably wasn't as certain as it now feels.
The third habit is to separate the decision from the result.
After something goes wrong, ask two different questions.
Given what I knew at the time, was it a sensible choice?
And was the bad result down to the decision, or down to luck?
Sometimes good decisions turn out badly, and bad decisions turn out well.
You can only improve if you judge the decision on its own merits.
The fourth habit is about kindness.
When a friend, a colleague or a family member makes a call that goes wrong, resist the urge to say you should have seen it coming.
Ask what they could reasonably have known at the time.
Often the honest answer is, not much more than they did.
This is the final episode of The Mind's Blind Spots.
Across the series, you've met confirmation bias, the sunk cost trap, anchoring, the fundamental attribution error, and now hindsight bias.
They share a common thread.
Our minds take shortcuts that usually work, but that quietly bend our view of evidence, money, other people and the past.
Let's recap this one.
Hindsight bias makes past events feel more predictable than they were, rewriting our memories and making us too quick to blame.
It leads us to judge decisions by their outcomes, which teaches us the wrong lessons.
To counter it, record your predictions before you know the result, imagine how things could have gone differently, and judge the decision separately from the luck.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Nixon study, how did students misremember their earlier predictions?
Answer. They remembered giving higher odds to events that actually happened.
Question two. What does Annie Duke call judging a decision purely by its outcome?
Answer. Resulting.
Question three. What's the most powerful fix for hindsight bias?
Answer. Record your predictions before you know the outcome.
That's the end of Hindsight Bias. Thanks for listening to the whole series.
